title: Why You Can't Hold Your Breath Forever
sources: Croatian freediver Budimir Šobat set the Guinness World Record for the longest breath held voluntarily (male): 24 min 37.36 s, Sisak, Croatia, 27 March 2021, after pre-breathing pure oxygen (Guinness World Records)

The urge to breathe is driven mainly by rising carbon dioxide (and falling pH) in the blood, sensed by chemoreceptors in the brainstem, not mainly by low oxygen (StatPearls, 'Physiology, Respiratory Drive'; Parkes 2006, Experimental Physiology)
During a long breath-hold, involuntary diaphragm contractions begin (the 'struggle phase') (Lindholm & Lundgren 2009, J Appl Physiol)

If a breath-hold continues, the person loses consciousness (hypoxic blackout); the brainstem then restarts automatic breathing, which is why holding your breath on land can't kill you but blackout underwater can drown you (Lindholm & Lundgren 2009; Divers Alert Network)

lines.text: When you hold your breath, it's not a lack of oxygen that makes you gasp.

lines.text: It's carbon dioxide building up in your blood.
Your brain senses it, and your diaphragm starts to twitch.

And the second you do, your brain takes over, and you start breathing again.
